One of the clearest examples is Ibn Sallām, who states that the poetry storytellers attributed to Tubbaʿ and Ḥimyar was fabricated.
He also says that Ibn Isḥāq and other transmitters of ancient stories like him invented this kind of poetry.
Abū al-Faraj, the author of al-Aghānī, also gives explicit accounts showing that these writers knew very well about the practice of fabricating poetry and attributing it to pre-Islamic figures.
Even writers of the Prophet’s biography treated the problem in much the same way.

Ibn Hishām, for example, reproduces poetry that Ibn Isḥāq attributes to ancient pre-Islamic figures while telling stories about them. But Ibn Hishām himself notes that many learned authorities rejected Ibn Isḥāq’s attribution of these poems.

Earlier scholars were also well aware of dishonest transmitters such as Ḥammād al-Rāwiya and Khalaf al-Aḥmar. They knew that such men sometimes attributed Islamic-period poetry to pre-Islamic poets, or even composed poems themselves and then presented them as pre-Islamic works.
These many references in the works of early Muslim scholars show, as we have said, that they recognized the phenomenon of poetic fabrication.
What they could not do was explain it critically by uncovering its historical basis and tracing it back to the real conditions that produced it.
This was not because of any personal intellectual failing on their part.
It was because of the historical conditions in which they lived. Those conditions had not yet given them the scientific tools of knowledge needed for that kind of criticism.

Among Orientalists, doubts about the authenticity of the surviving pre-Islamic poetry took a different form. They grew out of the modern development of methods for critically examining ancient texts and historical remains. The issue itself may first have been raised by Western Orientalists between 1850 and 1870.

From the beginning of the twentieth century, new Orientalist studies began looking for the religious, political, and cultural roots of the problem. Its social roots, however, were either ignored or treated only formally and superficially.

In 1920, the English Orientalist Margoliouth argued that none of the poetry known as pre-Islamic was actually pre-Islamic in origin. In his view, it was entirely Islamic: it had been composed by Muslim poets.

Other Orientalists, in studies dealing with particular aspects of Arab history before Islam, also questioned the authenticity of much of the surviving pre-Islamic poetry. Nöldeke, for example, argued that the Muslim transmitters who preserved this poetry had inserted the word “God” into it. According to him, they removed the names of pagan idols and replaced them with the name “God.” Where the original poem had mentioned al-Lāt, for example, “God” was later substituted in its place.

But another group of Orientalists accepted that pre-Islamic poetry was broadly authentic, while acknowledging that some poems may have been altered and that some surviving texts may have been fabricated.

The English Orientalist Rom Landau belonged to this group. He argued that the very close resemblance between pre-Islamic Bedouin poetry and Umayyad poetry was what led some critics to suggest that the two might actually belong to the same period—that is, that both were Umayyad. On this view, pre-Islamic poetry would have been a kind of harmless forgery produced by the Umayyads, without any personal motive behind it.
The French Orientalist Clément Huart, meanwhile, rejected the claim that the poetry of Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt was fabricated. He defended it as genuinely pre-Islamic.

This position deals with only one pre-Islamic poet, but it still challenges the general principle behind doubts about pre-Islamic poetry. The same argument used to question pre-Islamic poetry as a whole had also been used against the poetry of Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt: namely, that it reached the Islamic period only through oral transmitters.

We find something similar in the work of the German Orientalist Wellhausen. He disagreed with Nöldeke’s claim that Muslim transmitters replaced the names of pagan idols in pre-Islamic poetry with the name “God.”

Wellhausen denied that Muslim transmitters had made this change. In his view, the appearance of the name “God” in pre-Islamic poetry, without the names of particular idols, did not result from later editing. It reflected a habit of the pre-Islamic Arabs themselves. Out of respect for the gods, they avoided excessive or casual use of the names of particular deities. They therefore sometimes used the word “God” in place of the name of an idol. At that time, he argued, the word did not necessarily mean one particular god. It could simply mean “lord” or “deity.”

Again, this deals with only one specific issue. But it also challenges the blanket accusation that Muslim transmitters falsified pre-Islamic poetry. Instead, it points toward the need to study this poetry historically and to understand its relationship with pre-Islamic beliefs, ways of thinking, and customs.

There is, however, another approach among Orientalists that deserves particular attention when we consider the historical value of pre-Islamic poetry. This was the approach taken by the leading Russian Orientalist Krachkovsky.

After studying this poetry, Krachkovsky concluded that it gives us a truthful and faithful picture of Arab tribal life and of the environment in which the poetry arose. For that reason, he wrote, trustworthy specialists regarded pre-Islamic poetry as the most reliable source for learning about the conditions, customs, and traditions of the Arabs during the pre-Islamic period.
Krachkovsky reached this conclusion through his detailed study of Arabic poetry, published in 1924. His method comes very close to what we would call a scientific method.

He did not rule out the possibility that ancient texts had undergone some correction while they were being written down. He did not even rule out the possibility that entire works had been fabricated.

But he saw an objective reason why the Arabs of that period were unable to establish the authenticity of everything they recorded. They did not yet possess a historical method or a comparative method. As a result, they were often unable even to formulate the kinds of questions that we can now help to analyze.

Yet we face a different limitation when we study pre-Islamic poetry today. We can see only its static side, not its dynamic side. In other words, we have the poetry only in its finished form. We cannot see the earlier stages through which it developed. Whichever way we look at it, we are always looking at the same final picture.
Krachkovsky then raises another question: why is the language of pre-Islamic poetry so remarkably uniform?

Or was it created by later transmitters, or even by still later grammarians, who deliberately or unintentionally erased differences between dialects and turned the language into a single conventional form?

Or was the language itself an artificial literary language, developed before writing became widespread among certain tribes and adapted for poetry even though it differed from the everyday spoken language of most tribes?
Krachkovsky accepts the first possibility: he believes that the linguistic unity of pre-Islamic poetry was real.

The other two explanations—that the unity was created by transmitters or grammarians, or that the language of the poetry was an artificial literary language—do not, in his view, stand up to criticism. He states that most scholars had by then come to reject both.

On the first point, he accepts that two centuries of oral transmission after the rise of Islam must naturally have changed the language to some degree before the poems were finally written down. Linguists themselves may also have introduced changes unintentionally, especially since writing could not fully preserve pronunciation.

But Krachkovsky does not think these changes could have been either large or deliberate. Rhyme and meter, he argues, offered the strongest protection against major changes in the language of the poetry.
The evidence also shows, in his view, that grammarians did not erase differences between dialects. On the contrary, they made every effort to record and preserve them.

As for the second theory—that the language of the poetry was an artificial literary creation—Krachkovsky argues that this does not fit the actual lives of the poets, the simple content of their poetry, or its concern with camels, pasture, and similar features of everyday life. Under such conditions, an artificially manufactured poetic language would have been rather unusual.

He adds that the Arabian Peninsula preserved a broad linguistic unity until the ninth century. Grammarians believed that the Bedouins still spoke the pure language of ancient poetry in ordinary life. They turned to Bedouin speech not only to explain rare words found in poetry, but also to explain grammatical forms and sentence structures.

Krachkovsky therefore concludes that the language of this poetry shows a very high degree of mastery. That mastery itself points to a long period of development. Its maturity becomes especially clear, he says, when it is compared with the rhymed prose of the Qurʾān.
Krachkovsky continues in this critical and historical way until he reaches his conclusion about the historical value of pre-Islamic poetry.

In this poetry, he says, we possess the earliest surviving record of the Arabic language. For the history of this period, it is not merely the earliest source. In truth, it is the only surviving source we possess for many of the events it describes.
In his study of the traditions of the Arabic qaṣīda, Krachkovsky argues that the qaṣīda—the unified, stable, and structurally developed form of the Arabic ode—is what truly represents Arabic poetry.

The similarities between individual qaṣīdas, he argues, point to a long earlier history whose beginnings we cannot determine. Its roots must extend at least 150 years before the rise of Islam, which is the earliest period we can identify with any confidence.
He then argues that the traditions of the Arabic qaṣīda eventually became an established expression of public opinion.

After the rise of Islam, however, the Arabian Peninsula naturally stopped being the only center where these poetic traditions, with their established social functions, came together. Arabia became only one province among others. The new centers of political life became the main centers of these traditions, especially Syria and Iraq. These regions produced the great wealth of poetry of the Umayyad period: al-Akhṭal, Jarīr, al-Farazdaq, and others.
If we judged the poetry of these poets purely by its form, Krachkovsky says, we would find it difficult to say that it had been written after the rise of Islam.

We can therefore see that Krachkovsky approaches the problem of pre-Islamic poetry through a careful historical criticism. This leads him to the scholarly conclusion that the poetry is, in broad terms, authentic.
That, in general, is the position among Orientalists.
Among modern Arab scholars, pre-Islamic poetry has been approached in two sharply opposed ways.

The first was represented most clearly, openly, and boldly by Taha Hussein in his pioneering study, first published in 1926 under the title On Pre-Islamic Poetry, and then in a second edition in 1927 under the title On Pre-Islamic Literature.

The second approach was strongly represented by traditionalists and Arabists among historians and teachers of Arabic literature in universities, as well as by many writers and literary figures across the Arab world.
The difference between these two approaches is striking.

The first begins with doubt so extreme that it leads to the claim that “the overwhelming majority of what we call pre-Islamic literature has nothing to do with the pre-Islamic period at all. It was fabricated after the rise of Islam. It is therefore Islamic literature, reflecting the life, tendencies, and passions of Muslims far more than the life of the pre-Islamic Arabs.”

What remains of genuinely pre-Islamic literature, according to this view, is so small that it represents nothing and proves nothing. It cannot be relied upon to reconstruct a true literary picture of the pre-Islamic period.

Supporters of this approach go so far as to say that the poetry attributed to Imruʾ al-Qays, Ṭarafa, Ibn Kulthūm, or ʿAntara has nothing to do with these men. Instead, it was invented by transmitters, produced through changes in grammatical form, manufactured by grammarians, embellished by storytellers, or created by Qurʾānic commentators, hadith scholars, and theologians.
To understand the pre-Islamic period, they argue, we should not rely on the poetry attributed to it, but rather “on the Qurʾān on the one hand, and history and legend on the other.”
Nor, they say, should pre-Islamic poetry be used as evidence when interpreting the Qurʾān or hadith. Instead, the Qurʾān and hadith should be used to explain and interpret the poetry.

The second approach takes the opposite position. It simply accepts the authenticity of all poetry attributed to the pre-Islamic period, without doubt, reservation, or any real impulse to reconsider these attributions by using the more advanced methods of analysis available in our own time.
A third approach, however, has also appeared. It takes a middle position between these two extremes.

Perhaps its best representative—although those who follow this approach are still relatively few—is Jawād ʿAlī, author of an historical encyclopedia that can rightly be regarded as one of the most important modern additions to the Arabic library in its field: The History of the Arabs Before Islam.

When dealing with the attribution of pre-Islamic poetry, Jawād ʿAlī uses historical criticism and comparison. His research is objective in the sense that it does not begin from a fixed and absolute position that has already decided the answer in advance.
Take, for example, the religious and moral poetry attributed to Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt. Some of this poetry agrees with, or closely resembles, Islamic beliefs and sometimes even Qurʾānic language.
Jawād ʿAlī considers several possible explanations for this similarity. He then examines each one critically and historically, in light of the available reports and the historical circumstances.
He eventually reaches the view that “this similarity and agreement probably resulted from fabrication and invention.”
His reasoning begins with the fact that Umayya was undoubtedly a poet, since the transmitters unanimously agreed on this.

It also rests on the fact that Umayya “was in revolt against his people and angry with them because they worshipped idols. He had some belief in one God and some knowledge of Judaism and Christianity.”

But even so, Jawād ʿAlī does not believe that Umayya “knew all the details found in the Qurʾān and hadith about the Throne and the Footstool, God and His angels, the Resurrection, Paradise and Hell, judgment, reward and punishment, and similar matters.”

All these details, he argues, “are purely Islamic. They are not found in this form among the Jews, Christians, or ḥanīfs. So when they appear in Umayya’s poetry in specifically Islamic words and expressions, this is the work of a group of people in the Islamic period. They put these ideas into his mouth, just as they—or others—put similar things into the mouths of other poets and orators.

“They did this because they believed it would serve Islam. It would show that some people in the pre-Islamic period had been learned, that Islam had therefore not appeared as something completely strange, and that some of these people had known the unseen and expected an Arab prophet to appear soon. They were then said to have wished that they might live again in his time, or that their lives might be prolonged until they could meet him and become Muslims.
“Stories of this kind became popular and widespread, just as similar stories have spread in every religion.”
Jawād ʿAlī then supports this argument through a comparison of style.

He compares Umayya’s nonreligious poetry with the religious poetry attributed to him and uses the difference between them as a way of distinguishing genuine pre-Islamic poetry from later material falsely attributed to the pre-Islamic period.
On this basis, he argues that signs of fabrication in Umayya’s poetry can be seen “in its lack of consistency and in the differences in its style and spirit.

“When we look at the poetry attributed to him in praise, elegy, or other subjects not directly connected with religion, we find the style and texture of pre-Islamic poetry. But the religious and moralizing poems have a very different style. They are far removed from the known styles of pre-Islamic poets. Their language brings them closer to the poetry of strict jurists, Sufis, and Christian ascetics.

“It is therefore very far from the style of the pre-Islamic poets, even from the style of someone such as ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī and the other pre-Islamic poets close to the rise of Islam who were said to have been Christians.”
This example gives us an approach to pre-Islamic poetry that differs from both of the positions described above.
First, it differs from an approach that makes doubt the starting point and cause of research rather than something that may emerge as a result of research.

Second, it differs from an approach that begins with belief or certainty before any investigation has taken place, and then shapes the evidence so that the conclusion will fit the position already chosen in advance.
Taha Hussein states openly that in studying pre-Islamic literature he intends to adopt “the philosophical method introduced by Descartes for investigating the truths of things.”

“The basic rule of this method is that the researcher must free himself from everything he knew beforehand and begin his investigation with a mind completely empty of everything previously said about the subject. (...)

“Let us use this method when we study our ancient Arabic literature and its history. Let us approach this literature and its history after freeing ourselves from everything previously said about them, and after casting off all those heavy chains that bind our hands and feet, preventing free physical movement and preventing free intellectual movement as well.”
It is worth noting that Taha Hussein adopts the formal side of Descartes’s method of doubt.
It seems to me that he takes it apart from its specifically Cartesian philosophical content, or empties it of that content.
Descartes’s method of doubt rested, first, on his own understanding of what philosophy studies and, second, on his rationalist theory of knowledge.

On the first point, Descartes believed that philosophy was concerned only with nature and the human being. In other words, when he developed his method of doubt, the idea of “God” did not, in his view, form part of the subject matter of philosophy.

This is why he argued that the human mind had to be cleared of every belief it had previously accepted. He called this process “doubt” and carried it to the point of saying that we must doubt all the knowledge that has accumulated in human consciousness over its long history.
On the second point—his rationalist theory of knowledge—Descartes also argued that the mind had to be cleared of knowledge that reached it through the senses.
In his view, no quality of things known through the senses could give us true knowledge.

This followed from his rationalist theory of knowledge, which rejected the idea that reliable knowledge could be built on sense experience. He denied that knowledge begins with the senses—that we move from sensory experience toward truth and finally arrive at basic principles, as Bacon had argued.
